section.title: Rise Up and Help Us
section.sectionRationale: A communal lament of the sons of Korah, this psalm moves from confident rehearsal of God's past victories to bewildered protest at present defeat, refusing to explain the nation's suffering as deserved punishment. Paul later cites verse 22 in Romans 8:36, showing that unexplained suffering for God's sake belongs to the pattern of the whole people of God, joined to Christ.
section.thesis: Israel remembers how God alone won their fathers' battles, yet now suffers crushing defeat and reproach despite unbroken covenant loyalty, so the psalm entrusts this unexplained suffering to God's steadfast love rather than to any theory that the sufferers deserved it, a protest Paul takes up on behalf of all who suffer for Christ's sake.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the fathers' victories won by God alone, verses 1-3; present trust that God alone still saves, verses 4-8; the bewildering complaint of rejection and reproach, verses 9-16; the protest of unbroken covenant loyalty even unto slaughter, verses 17-22; and the final cry for God to wake and redeem, verses 23-26.

units.label: We have heard with our ears, O God
units.note: the fathers' victories, won by God alone

verses.text: We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have told us the work You did in their days, in the days of old.
With Your hand You drove out the nations and planted our fathers there; You crushed the peoples and cast them out.

For it was not by their sword that they took the land; their arm did not bring them victory. It was by Your right hand, Your arm, and the light of Your face, 
because You favored them.

units.label: You are my King, O God
units.note: present trust that God alone still saves

verses.text: You are my King, O God, who ordains victories for Jacob.
Through You we repel our foes; through Your name we trample our enemies.
For I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me.
For You save us from our enemies; You put those who hate us to shame.
In God we have boasted all day long, and Your name we will praise forever. Selah

units.label: But You have rejected and humbled us
units.note: the bewildering complaint of present defeat

verses.text: But You have {{zanach|rejected}} and humbled us; You no longer go forth with our armies.
You have made us retreat from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered us.
You have given us up as sheep to be devoured; You have scattered us among the nations.
You sell Your people for nothing; no profit do You gain from their sale.
You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us.
You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples.
All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face,
at the voice of the scorner and reviler, because of the enemy, bent on revenge.

units.label: Yet for Your sake we face death all day long
units.note: unbroken covenant loyalty even unto slaughter

verses.text:
All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You 
or betrayed Your covenant.
Our hearts have not turned back; our steps have not strayed from Your path.
But You have crushed us in the lair of jackals; You have covered us with deepest darkness.
If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god,
would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart?
Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.

units.label: Rise up; be our help
units.note: the final cry for God to wake and redeem

verses.text: Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever.
Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?
For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth.
Rise up; be our help! Redeem us on account of Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}.

zanach.gloss: To reject, spurn, or cast off. The psalmist accuses God of this action against His own people, a bold complaint that names the felt experience of abandonment without concluding that God has broken His covenant faithfulness.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion, God's loyal love that binds Him to His promises. The psalm's final appeal rests entirely on this word, asking God to act consistently with His own covenant character rather than on any merit of the sufferers.

basic.context: This communal lament, sung by the whole nation rather than one person, remembers how God alone, not the sword, won the land for their fathers, yet now confesses a bewildering present defeat, plunder, and mockery among the nations despite the people's unbroken loyalty to the covenant. It ends by begging God to wake up and act for the sake of His own steadfast love.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm refuses the simple explanation that suffering always proves hidden sin. The psalmist insists Israel has not forgotten God or turned from His path, verses 17-18, so the suffering remains unexplained even as it is fully entrusted to God rather than resolved by human reasoning.
basic.originalLanguages: God is charged with having zanach, rejected or cast off, His people, verse 9, an unusually bold verb for a lament directed at God Himself. Yet the psalm's whole appeal in the final verse rests on chesed, God's own steadfast, covenant loving devotion, the very quality the psalmist insists God has not truly abandoned.
basic.typology: Verse 22, being counted as sheep for the slaughter while remaining faithful to God, is quoted directly by Paul in Romans 8:36 concerning those united to Christ, showing that unexplained suffering for God's sake belongs to the pattern of Christ's own people, who are nonetheless more than conquerors through Him who loved them, Romans 8:37.
basic.christ: Paul quotes Psalm 44:22 word for word in Romans 8:36 to describe the sufferings of those in Christ, immediately answering it with 'in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us,' Romans 8:37, showing that this psalm's unresolved lament finds its resolution not in an explanation but in the unbreakable love of God secured in Christ.
basic.god: God is shown as the true and only source of victory, whose past deeds the fathers told of, yet whose present silence and apparent sleep the psalmist dares to name honestly, all while still resting every hope on God's own covenant loving devotion rather than any explanation of the suffering.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8:36-37 quotes this psalm's verse 22 directly, applying its unexplained suffering to those in Christ and answering it with the certainty of Christ's love. Isaiah 53:7 pictures the Servant led like a sheep to the slaughter. 2 Corinthians 4:8-11 echoes the same pattern of being given over to death for Jesus' sake without being forsaken.
basic.oneStory: Israel's honest protest, unexplained suffering held together with unbroken covenant loyalty and hope in God's steadfast love, anticipates the sufferings of Christ's own people, whom Paul describes in the very words of this psalm, yet who are more than conquerors through Him who loved them and gave Himself for them.

context.literary:
Psalm 44 is built as a hinge. Verses 1 to 8 look back, and every verb of victory has God as its subject: You drove out, You planted, You crushed, You favored. Verse 9 then opens with a stark 'But', and from there to verse 22 the same second person, 'You', becomes the subject of every verb of defeat: You have rejected, You have made us retreat, You have given us up, You sell Your people. The poem is a mirror. The God who did everything for the fathers is now the one who does everything against the children, and the poet's shock is in the symmetry.

The pronouns are also worth watching. The psalm begins with 'we' and 'our fathers', slips to a singular 'I' and 'my' in verses 4 to 6, returns to 'we' for the recital of defeat, and comes back to 'my disgrace' in verse 15. It is a national lament voiced by a leader, probably the king or a Levite speaking for the people, and the switch between plural and singular shows how the individual stands for the community.

The third movement, verses 17 to 22, is the claim of innocence. It is hedged by conditionals: 'If we had forgotten the name of our God', verse 20, followed by the rhetorical question of verse 21. The poet builds a small legal argument. If the charge were idolatry, God would have found out, since He knows the secrets of the heart. But the punishment has fallen without a charge, and the verdict is 'for Your sake', verse 22.

The last stanza breaks into commands that are startlingly blunt: 'Wake up', 'Arise', 'Rise up; be our help'. Between the recital of the past and these final verbs, the poet uses the language of the very first verse of the psalm, 'the days of old', against God, asking Him to be who He has been. The psalm has no answer. It ends on a plea and on the word chesed, which is the only ground the poet can stand on.
context.historical:
The heading assigns the psalm to the sons of Korah and calls it a maskil, which the BSB footnote takes as a musical or liturgical term. Nothing in the text names a king, a battle or a year. Verses 9 to 16 describe a military defeat in which the army no longer goes out with God, the people are plundered and scattered among the nations, and the neighbours mock. That fits several moments in Israel's history, and interpreters have proposed the disaster of Josiah's death, a defeat in the days of the divided monarchy, the Babylonian invasions and the exile, or, in some modern proposals, the persecution of the second century before Christ. The text does not settle the matter, and the psalm's power as a prayer owes something to that openness.

The first section leans on the conquest traditions. Verse 2 has God drive out the nations and plant Israel in the land, language taken from the Exodus and Joshua tradition; Joshua 24:12 is a close parallel, where God says that it was not Israel's sword or bow that won the land. The phrase 'the light of Your face' in verse 3 echoes the priestly blessing, 'may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you', Numbers 6:25.

The curses of the covenant lie in the background of the complaint. Deuteronomy 28:25 warns that if Israel does not obey, the Lord will cause them to be defeated before their enemies, and Leviticus 26:33 threatens scattering among the nations. The psalmist experiences exactly these conditions and denies that he has broken the covenant. That is what makes the psalm dangerous: it takes the formula that Israel had been taught for explaining calamity and finds that it does not fit.

Sheep and slaughter were everyday images in a pastoral and sacrificial world. To be sold 'for nothing', verse 12, echoes the language of a slave market, and the same phrase appears in Isaiah 52:3, where God says His people were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money. The psalmist stands on that hope.
context.canonical:
Psalm 44 opens a tight run of Korahite psalms, 44 to 49, and it is the darkest of them. The Psalter contains only a few national laments like it, among them Psalms 60, 74, 79, 80 and 89. Psalm 89 comes at the end of Book III with a similar reversal: the Lord who swore loyalty to David has now rejected and spurned His anointed. Psalm 44 is an earlier voice of the same complaint.

The psalm answers a lesson the Bible has been teaching. The blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 invited Israel to read her history as a ledger of obedience and consequence, and the prophets often did. The book of Job and Psalm 73 press against that reading. Job is described as blameless, Job 1:8, and yet suffers; Psalm 44 is the national version of the Job problem. The Bible does not throw out the covenant account, since Daniel's prayer confesses that Israel has sinned and is covered with shame, Daniel 9:5-7. It keeps both, and Psalm 44 is the place where the innocent voice is allowed to speak.

The New Testament quotes the psalm once, and decisively. Paul cites verse 22 in Romans 8:36, 'For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered', and then answers it: 'No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.' Paul gathers the psalm's unexplained suffering into the family of Christ. The BSB footnote to Psalm 44:22 records that it is cited in Romans 8:36. Second Corinthians 4:8-11 carries the same thought of being consigned to death for Jesus' sake without being forsaken.

The psalm's last cry echoes in the Gospels: Jesus is asleep in a storm and the disciples wake Him with 'Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?', Mark 4:38. The language of the sleeping God is answered there.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The composer, a Korahite singer, wrote for public worship in a time of national disaster. He wanted the congregation to be able to say aloud what many were thinking, and to do it in the presence of God and not behind His back. The psalm gives the community permission to protest.

He also wanted to keep the people from two errors. One is despair, the conclusion that God has broken covenant and that the old stories are false. The recital of verses 1 to 8 stops that: it holds the past up as evidence of who God is. The other is the neat theology that says every defeat proves sin. The middle of the psalm resists that. The community is not asked to invent a hidden guilt to explain the loss. It is asked to say honestly that it cannot see one and to trust God with the question.

The author's argument is that the right response to unexplained suffering is prayer that leans on God's character. The final word is not a theory but chesed. Redemption is requested 'on account of Your loving devotion', which means that the appeal rests not on the people's record but on God's. The hearers are to leave the psalm knowing that when they cannot understand what God is doing, they can still stand on who He is.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a defeat and a protest. It does not tell Israel to expect defeat, nor does it say that faithful people are always defeated. Other passages promise blessing to obedience, and the psalm itself remembers times of victory. It is a description of one hard chapter and a permission to pray in it.

It is also important to see that the claim of innocence in verses 17 to 18 is the people's claim. The psalm records it and does not endorse it as a final verdict on Israel, whose history the prophets tell differently. A reader should not take these verses as proof that any given community of believers is blameless when it suffers, and certainly not as an excuse to dismiss self examination. The psalm is best used by a sufferer who has looked at his own conscience and found no sin sufficient to explain the trouble.

What the psalm prescribes is the boldness of the final verses. 'Wake up', 'Arise', 'Redeem us' are commands directed at God, but they are set in a context of trust and covenant. Scripture sanctions that kind of prayer. It does not sanction accusing God of wrong. Paul's use of verse 22 shows the safe application: suffering for Christ's sake is not a sign that God's love has failed, and no trouble can separate believers from that love, Romans 8:35-39.

debates.question: Can the people's claim of innocence be true, given Israel's record?

views.label: A sincere claim of covenant loyalty
views.case: The people say they have not forgotten God or turned to a foreign god, verses 17 to 20. On this reading the psalm is set in a time of real faithfulness, perhaps under a reforming king, and the suffering that follows is a real puzzle, like Job's. The text gives no confession, and nothing in it hints that the claim is a lie.

views.label: Relative innocence
views.case: The claim is limited to the specific charges of idolatry and disloyalty, not to sinlessness. The psalm asserts that they have not abandoned the covenant, which is compatible with ordinary failing. The stress is that the punishment is out of proportion to any visible offence.

views.label: An honest but incomplete self judgment
views.case: Some read the psalm alongside the prophets, who said that the people did not see their own sin, and treat the claim as the way the people felt rather than a final assessment. Daniel 9:5-7 shows that a later generation looked at the same history and confessed.

debates.bearing: The psalm is recorded as Scripture as a legitimate prayer, and the text does not correct its claim. The wise use is to pray it when conscience is clear on the points named, and to hold it with the humility Daniel shows.

debates.question: What is the setting of the psalm, and does it matter?

views.label: A pre-exilic military defeat
views.case: The army 'no longer goes forth', verse 9, and the enemy plunders. Such words fit a battle in the days of the kings, perhaps a defeat like the one that killed Josiah.

views.label: The Babylonian exile
views.case: Verse 11 has the people scattered among the nations, and verses 13 to 14 describe a people become a byword. This suits the aftermath of 587 BC, though the claim of covenant loyalty is harder to reconcile with the prophets' account of that era.

views.label: A later persecution
views.case: Some scholars place the psalm in the second century before Christ, when faithful Jews were killed for their loyalty. The phrase 'for Your sake' in verse 22 suits martyrdom. The heading's ascription to the Korahites, however, and the psalm's place in the collection make an earlier date more natural to many.

debates.bearing: The uncertainty leaves the psalm open for use by every generation. Its argument does not rest on the date.

study.originalLanguages:
The lexicon word for 'rejected' in verse 9 is zanach, the verb that also opens the cry of Psalm 74:1, 'Why have You rejected us forever', and returns in verse 23 of this psalm: 'Do not reject us forever.' It is a word for casting off. The poet uses it in the bold assertion of verse 9 and then in the plea of verse 23, taking the accusation and turning it into a request that God would not do what he says God has done.

The sheep of verses 11 and 22 are described differently. In verse 11 the Hebrew has sheep 'of food', that is, sheep destined to be eaten; in verse 22 they are sheep 'of slaughter'. The image moves from consumption to sacrifice, and the second is the one Paul quotes. Paul quotes from the Septuagint, which stays close to the Hebrew.

Verse 12 has God 'sell' His people 'for nothing'. The verb makar is the standard verb for selling, used of Joseph, Genesis 37:28, and of Israel given over to enemies, Judges 2:14. To sell for no price is to say that the loss was not even a fair exchange. The complaint is that God gained nothing. Isaiah 52:3 uses the same idea with hope: 'You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.'

The phrase in verse 19 rendered 'lair of jackals' translates a place of desolation. The BSB footnote notes an alternative reading, 'serpents or dragons'. Jeremiah 9:11 calls Jerusalem after destruction 'a haunt for jackals', which supports the desert reading; the footnote's alternative would make the phrase a picture of chaos monsters. Either way the sense is a wilderness of death.

In verse 21 God 'knows the secrets of the heart'. The final appeal of verse 26 uses padah, to redeem, an important verb of ransom, and joins it with 'on account of Your loving devotion'. The phrase 'for Your sake' in verse 22 gives the people's suffering a reason in God, and the closing 'on account of Your loving devotion' gives their hope a reason in God as well. The last word of the psalm therefore answers the hardest word, and the pivot is the character of God.

In verse 23 the command 'Wake up' uses the verb for rousing someone from sleep. God is pictured as sleeping, a bold anthropomorphism that contrasts with Psalm 121:4, where the Protector of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. Psalm 78:65 uses the image of the Lord waking as from sleep to defeat His foes. The psalmist does not mean that God is literally asleep but that He has been inactive, and he is willing to speak like that.

typology.type: The people counted as sheep for slaughter, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: Israel, loyal to the covenant and killed for God's sake, is a picture of the people of God under persecution. Paul applies verse 22 to Christians in Romans 8:36, and Hebrews 11:36-38 lists the faithful who were mocked, flogged, stoned and put to death, of whom the world was not worthy. The pattern finds its head in Christ, who 'was led like a sheep to the slaughter', Acts 8:32, quoting Isaiah 53:7. The type escalates because the sheep in the psalm suffer without knowing why, whereas the Lamb suffers for a purpose, John 1:29. It falls short in that Israel's suffering could not atone; His does.

The people cry to a God who seems to sleep while they perish. In the boat on the Sea of Galilee the disciples wake Jesus, who is literally asleep on a cushion, and say, 'Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?', Mark 4:38. He rebukes the wind and sea, and the storm goes quiet. The scene does not fulfil the psalm as a prediction, but it enacts its plea: the Lord rises and helps. The correspondence is limited, since a storm on a lake is not a national catastrophe, and the greater rising is the resurrection, when God raises His Son, Acts 2:24.

The nation feels cast off by God and covered with shame among the nations. Jesus takes the most extreme form of that experience when He cries, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46, and endures reproach outside the camp, Hebrews 13:12-13. Where Israel felt rejected without cause, Christ was made a curse in the place of others, Galatians 3:13. The result is that those united to Him can be sure that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all' and will also 'freely give us all things', Romans 8:32. The type is limited because Israel's rejection was in part chastisement, while His was substitutionary.

typology.type: Victory not by sword or arm, verses 3 and 6
typology.fulfillment: The fathers took the land 'by Your right hand, Your arm', and the psalmist says he does not trust his bow. The pattern of victory by God alone comes to its fullest in the cross, where Christ, weaponless, triumphed over the powers, Colossians 2:15. Believers fight with weapons that are not of the flesh, 2 Corinthians 10:4, and Paul's 'more than conquerors' in Romans 8:37 belongs to the same line. The type is limited by its military frame; the enemies of the new covenant are not nations but sin, death and the devil.

study.christ:
Psalm 44 reaches Christ most directly through Paul. In Romans 8 Paul builds an argument that moves from the Spirit and adoption to the certainty of God's love, and at its climax he asks, 'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?' Then he quotes the psalm: 'For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.' The psalm is brought into the middle of the gospel to prove that suffering is not a sign of God's rejection. The answer comes at once: 'No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us', Romans 8:37. Paul reads a lament that has no answer in the psalm and gives it the answer of the cross.

The psalm's accusations against God also come to rest on Christ. The psalmist says God has rejected His people and sold them for nothing. Paul asks earlier in the same chapter how God could fail to freely give us all things when He 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all', Romans 8:32. What the psalm cannot explain, that God gives up His people, is explained in the giving up of the Son. He was rejected so that they are not. On the cross, Jesus cries the opening of Psalm 22, but the experience of Psalm 44, being made a reproach and a mockery among the people, is also His, as the crowd at Golgotha jeers.

The psalm also leads to Christ in the figure of the righteous sufferer. The people claim innocence and yet are counted as sheep for slaughter. Only one person could make that claim without qualification. Isaiah 53:7 presents a servant led like a lamb to the slaughter, and Acts 8:32 applies it to Jesus. Peter says that when He suffered, He made no threats, 1 Peter 2:23. The psalm's sheep and the Lamb are joined by the same image, though the difference is decisive: the sheep are killed, the Lamb takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29.

A caution: Psalm 44 is not a prophecy of the cross in the way of Psalm 22. The psalm is first the prayer of Israel, and it becomes the prayer of Christ's people because of union with Him. The bridge is the way the New Testament itself uses the text, and where it does not, we should not press the correspondence.
study.god:
The psalm displays a God who acts in history. Verses 1 to 3 rehearse what the fathers told: God's hand drove out the nations, His arm brought victory, His face shone on them 'because You favored them'. The reason given for His favour is not their strength or merit but His own delight. That is a theology of grace in an Old Testament song. The people did not earn the land, and the psalm says so.

The psalm equally shows God as king. Verse 4 declares, 'You are my King, O God, who ordains victories for Jacob.' Kingship means that victory and defeat are both under His hand, which is exactly why the defeat troubles the singer. If God were one power among many, defeat would be no puzzle. Because He is sovereign, the poet lays the loss at His feet. The doctrine of divine sovereignty is here not a comfortable theory but the ground of a painful question.

The psalm shows a God who is not answerable to human accounting. The poet does not know why God has acted, and the psalm does not tell us. God is not obliged to give reasons, and the wise response is not to invent them but to keep praying. At the same time, the God of the psalm is one who knows 'the secrets of the heart', verse 21. He is not fooled by claims of loyalty, and the poet knows it. The claim of innocence is made before an all-knowing judge.

The God of the psalm is also covenant-keeping. The end of the psalm rests on His chesed. He has bound Himself in love to Israel, and the poet takes the risk of holding Him to that. This is the pattern of biblical faith: to accuse God is not to abandon Him but to insist that He be Himself.

The psalm holds together God's power and His apparent absence, His past faithfulness and present silence. It does not resolve them. It teaches that mystery does not cancel confidence.

For worship, the psalm gives the church words for seasons when praise is hard. It shows that the honest lament of a suffering community is itself an act of faith, that God is big enough to receive our complaints, and that the last appeal in every darkness is not a theory of suffering but the steadfast love of the King.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes Psalm 44:22 to say that trouble, danger and sword do not mean God has stopped loving His people, and then declares that nothing in all creation can separate believers from His love in Christ. The psalm's unexplained suffering is held inside an unbreakable love.

God reminds Israel that He drove out the two Amorite kings, but not by their own sword or bow. It is the background to Psalm 44:3 and 44:6, where the psalmist confesses that victory came by God's arm and not by weapons.

The priestly blessing asks that the Lord make His face shine upon His people. Psalm 44:3 speaks of 'the light of Your face' as the source of victory, and 44:24 laments that God hides His face. The two verses show what is lost when the blessing seems withdrawn.

God says His people were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money. It answers Psalm 44:12, where God is said to sell His people for nothing. The prophet takes the same image of a bad bargain and turns it into a promise of free redemption.

After Israel's rebellion, 'the Lord awoke as from sleep'. This is the same picture of a God roused to fight that Psalm 44:23 requests. Together they show that biblical prayer may address God as if He has been still, in the hope that He will act.

The Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. It stands against the plea of Psalm 44:23, and the tension is instructive: the psalm speaks from the experience of the sufferer, while Psalm 121 speaks from the truth about God. Both belong in the Psalter.

The Lord calls Job blameless and upright, and Job then suffers. Psalm 44 shares the problem of suffering with a clear conscience, and neither book explains it. Both leave God free and the sufferer honest.

The Servant is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open His mouth. The sheep of Psalm 44:22 are killed without a word of explanation; the Servant's silence gives their suffering a place in God's saving plan, as Acts 8:32 confirms.

Paul says believers are hard pressed but not crushed, persecuted but not forsaken, always consigned to death for Jesus' sake so that His life may be revealed. It shows the pattern of Psalm 44:22 as the daily reality of apostolic ministry.

Daniel confesses that Israel has sinned and is covered with shame. It stands beside Psalm 44:17-18 as a different reading of the same history, and shows that the Bible allows both the plea of innocence and the confession of sin.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 44 begins with a memory of the conquest, when God planted Israel in the land, and ends with a cry from the ruins. Between those poles lies much of the Old Testament. The garden of Genesis 2 is the first planting, and the land is a second. Just as Adam was sent out of the garden, Israel is scattered from the land, and the psalm's question is why the people who were planted must be uprooted. The Bible's answer has two sides. The prophets say that the people broke the covenant and reaped the curses. The psalm says that there are times when the suffering cannot be traced to a visible crime. Both are true, and the story cannot be told without them.

The psalm also sets up a question that only Christ can answer: how can God's people suffer while God is faithful and while they are faithful to Him? The answer is given in stages. Job and the psalms show the question. Isaiah 53 shows a servant who suffers and whose suffering is redemptive. The cross shows that the greatest suffering is God's own act of love, and Romans 8:32 says that He did not spare His own Son. Once that has happened, the suffering of His people is no longer a sign of rejection but a sharing in Christ's path, Philippians 3:10 and 2 Corinthians 4:10.

The last cry of the psalm, 'Rise up; be our help! Redeem us', is answered in the resurrection and in the coming of the Spirit. It continues to be prayed by the persecuted church, and by the martyrs under the altar in Revelation 6:9-10, who ask how long. The story ends with the answer. In the new creation God wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4, and there is no more sword, no more sheep for slaughter, and no more reproach. The people who felt sold for nothing are called 'a people for God's own possession', 1 Peter 2:9, ransomed at the price of the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 5:9. The one who seemed to sleep is the one who dwells with them, Revelation 21:3, and His steadfast love is finally seen for what it always was.

quiz.q: According to verses 1-3, how did the fathers actually take the land?

options.text: Not by their own sword, but by God's right hand, arm, and favor.
options.note: The psalm insists victory came only through God's favor, not human military strength.

options.text: By forming a strong military alliance with neighboring nations.
options.note: The text explicitly denies human means; it credits God's hand and favor alone.

options.text: By their own superior weapons and numbers.
options.note: The psalm directly denies this, crediting God's arm and favor rather than the sword.

options.text: Through a peace treaty rather than conquest.
options.note: The land was taken through conquest, but the point of the text is that God, not the sword, gave the victory.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist insist about the nation's conduct despite present suffering, verses 17-18?

options.text: They have not forgotten God or betrayed His covenant, nor turned back from His path.
options.note: The psalm explicitly denies covenant unfaithfulness as the cause of the suffering.

options.text: They openly admit to having worshiped foreign gods.
options.note: The text explicitly denies this in verse 20; it is a hypothetical the psalmist rules out.

options.text: They acknowledge some minor lapses but nothing serious.
options.note: The psalmist claims total, not partial, faithfulness, inviting God Himself to verify it.

options.text: They are uncertain whether they have sinned or not.
options.note: The psalmist is not uncertain; he confidently asserts unbroken loyalty to the covenant.

quiz.q: Which verse of this psalm does Paul quote directly in Romans 8:36?

options.text: Verse 22, 'we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.'
options.note: Paul applies this exact line to believers suffering for Christ's sake, answering it with assured love in verse 37.

options.text: Verse 3, about the land taken by God's hand.
options.note: Paul's quotation in Romans 8:36 is verse 22, concerning suffering, not the conquest of the land.

options.text: Verse 8, about boasting in God all day long.
options.note: This verse expresses praise, not the suffering language Paul quotes in Romans 8:36.

options.text: Verse 26, the final cry for redemption.
options.note: This is the psalm's closing plea, but the specific verse Paul quotes in Romans 8:36 is verse 22.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do in the closing verses, 23 and 26?

options.text: Wake up, arise, and redeem them because of His loving devotion.
options.note: The psalm ends with an urgent plea for God to act, grounded entirely in His covenant loving devotion, chesed.

options.text: Explain clearly why the suffering has happened.
options.note: The psalm never asks for an explanation; it asks God to act, not to account for the suffering.

options.text: Grant them victory through a stronger army.
options.note: The plea is for God Himself to arise and redeem, not for greater military strength.

options.text: Remove all future possibility of suffering.
options.note: The specific request is immediate help and redemption now, not a guarantee against all future suffering.

quiz.q: What is this psalm's overall stance toward the nation's suffering?

options.text: It is an honest protest that refuses to explain the suffering as deserved punishment, entrusting it instead to God's steadfast love.
options.note: The psalm holds bold complaint and unwavering covenant trust together without resolving why the suffering has come.

options.text: It calmly assumes the suffering must be deserved punishment for hidden sin.
options.note: The psalm explicitly denies this explanation in verses 17-21.

options.text: It abandons faith in God altogether because of the suffering.
options.note: The psalm never abandons faith; its entire appeal rests on God's covenant loving devotion.

options.text: It treats the suffering as unimportant and moves on quickly.
options.note: The suffering is described at painful length, verses 9-22, and taken with total seriousness.

questions: The psalmist remembers God's past faithfulness even while confessing bewildering present suffering. What past evidence of God's faithfulness do you return to when your present circumstances feel confusing or painful?

This psalm refuses to explain suffering as always being deserved punishment. Have you ever assumed, wrongly, that someone's suffering, or your own, must be traceable to hidden sin? How does this psalm's honesty challenge that assumption?

The psalmist boldly tells God 'You have rejected and humbled us' while still trusting His covenant love. What would it look like for you to bring an equally honest complaint to God without abandoning your trust in Him?

Paul quotes this psalm's verse 22 for Christians suffering for Christ's sake, answering it with assured victory in Romans 8:37. How does knowing that unexplained suffering can still be lived within the love of Christ change how you carry your own hardships?
The psalm ends with an urgent, unresolved cry, 'Rise up, be our help.' What unresolved situation in your life most needs that same honest, hope-filled cry today?

translationNotes.note: The light of Your face is a Hebrew idiom for God's favorable, personal presence, contrasted here with mere military strength as the true source of the fathers' victories.
Rejected renders zanach, a strong verb of spurning or casting off, an unusually direct accusation for a lament addressed to God Himself.
Sheep to be slaughtered is quoted word for word by Paul in Romans 8:36, applying this ancient communal lament to the sufferings of those united to Christ.
Loving devotion renders chesed, God's steadfast covenant love, the sole ground on which the psalm's final appeal for redemption rests.
